newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's main opposition says committed to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's main opposition says committed to EMU.

text.p: Ireland's main opposition Fianna Fail party, which expects to be the main partner in a coalition government after elections on Friday, said on Tuesday it was firmly committed to joining a single EU currency from the start.
"The principle of joining EMU (economic and monetary union) in the first wave should not, I believe, be an issue," Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern told a news conference.
"If we fulfil the Maastricht criteria, which we do, we are legally committed to becoming members," he said.
"It would send very wrong signals to Europe, and would suggest that we were to all intents and purposes an economic satellite of Britain if we were to seek to renege on our commitment."

Despite warnings by some economists that joining EMU would be dangerous for Ireland's economy if Britain stayed out, Ahern said Ireland should be in the first wave whatever Britain did. But he said he was encouraged by what he saw as signs that Britain would join the single currency.
"It is reasonably clear that the new British government are preparing the ground for participation in EMU. Whether to begin with or later is not yet clear," he said.
This is encouraging from an Irish point of view as it would imply that there will probably only be a short transition period that will have to be managed for two or three years."

Some economists have warned that if the euro is relatively weak against sterling, Ireland could face an inflationary boom because of its strong trade links with Britain. But Ahern said this was not a danger at present.

"A trade-weighted effective index is still a couple of points higher than 12 months ago according to the central bank, so there is no overall reason why from that point of view inflation should take off," he said.
"If the euro went even lower against sterling, that would be an opportunity not a problem for the exposed sector."

Ahern said he believed EMU would go ahead on schedule, despite a landslide for the socialist party in France's elections and a row between the German government and Bundesbank over the revaluation of gold reserves.

"There is in Europe a huge political commitment to EMU," he said. "I think it is a mistake to read recent political upheavals and controversy in France and Germany as meaning that it could all be about to unravel."

Fianna Fail hopes to form the next Irish government in coalition with the Progressive Democrats. An opinion poll in the Sunday Independent newspaper put support for Fianna Fail at 40 percent, with the Progressive Democrats on six percent. The Progressive Democrats are seen as being more cautious on EMU than Fianna Fail.
Support for the three parties of the ruling "rainbow coalition" was put at 42 percent. The ruling coalition is also committed to being in the first wave of EMU.
Ahern attacked the public spending policies of the ruling coalition, promising to take a tougher line if he won power.

"A strong cohesive Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat government, that will pursue a firm economic policy and limit public spending, is far more likely to make a success of early membership of EMU than a rainbow that refuses to set any serious limits on spending and that is bound sooner or later to run the country into serious difficulties."
Ahern said he would stick to a "hard fiscal strategy", saying it was the right course for Ireland even if EMU was delayed or abandoned.
He said he would aim to cut Ireland's debt/GDP ratio to 50 percent within seven years, and to cut taxes.

"Economic competition will become even more intense in EMU," Ahern said. "The Irish economy could not be regarded as fully competitive as long as we maintain high personal tax rates...Action on reducing taxes is a vital component of Ireland's EMU strategy."
